about: The factory (WS-27): our analysis per target company, rendered by people/indi/pages.mjs. The sourced facts (name, what it does, sources) come from data/companies.json; everything here is analysis, not the company's statements. Written by dev@web-summit.indi.
intro: For every company we want to meet at Web Summit: what it does, the risks it faces from AI agents, and how RiskMandate helps, each in normal terms and in lay terms side by side. To help the team understand what we are doing and why each conversation matters.

riskmandate.reach: Everything an AI agent can actually access or affect: systems, data, actions, connectors.
riskmandate.mandate: What the business has authorised it to do: the task, the scope, the purpose.
riskmandate.gap: What the agent could do but was never asked to. This is where the risk lives.
riskmandate.barriers: The real controls that stop unwanted behaviour, each with evidence: technical, rule or review.
riskmandate.provenance: Who owns the agent, who reviewed it, and which version is running.
riskmandate.n: RiskMandate gives every AI agent an Agent Behaviour Policy: a factual record of its Reach, its Mandate, the Gap between them, the Barriers that hold, and its Provenance, ending in a Licence to Operate. Operators, security, leadership and insurers each read the same record from their own side. The line: know their reach, define their mandate, control the gap.
riskmandate.l: An AI agent is like a new employee with a master key. RiskMandate writes down which doors the key opens, which rooms the employee is actually meant to be in, and what stops them wandering into the others. Then everyone, from the boss to the insurer, can see it on one page.

companies.tagline: Cisco's incubator and developer platform for agentic AI: building the plumbing that agents will run on.
flow: DevNet: a developer platform for agentic AI
Open-source agent projects for the community
companies.what_n: Through Outshift and DevNet, Cisco gives developers open-source building blocks for agents that talk to each other and to the network.
companies.what_l: Cisco builds the roads and traffic lights of the internet. Now it is building the roads AI assistants will drive on.

risks.n: Agents built on shared infrastructure can reach systems and other agents far beyond their task, across company boundaries.
risks.l: Once on the motorway, a car can drive anywhere, not just to the shop.

risks.n: Open-source agent components spread fast; each adopter inherits defaults that may grant more reach than they need.
risks.l: Free car kits are great, but everyone builds them with the same loose bolts.

risks.n: In multi-agent systems, responsibility for an action is split between builders, operators and the platform.
risks.l: After a pile-up, who was driving?

helps.reach: Every system and agent a DevNet-built agent can contact.
helps.mandate: The task its owner approved.
helps.gap: Connections the agent has but its task never uses.
helps.barriers: Network controls and agent identities, named as evidence.
helps.provenance: Which team built it, on which open-source version.
helps.n: RiskMandate offers the agent-infrastructure community a common record per agent: a behaviour policy that travels with the agent across the network. Open projects could ship with an example policy, so every adopter starts with a stated mandate.
helps.l: Cisco builds the roads; RiskMandate is the driving licence that says where each car may go.

companies.opener: You are building the roads for agents. Could every agent on them carry a licence that says where it may go?

companies.tagline: An open-source gatekeeper for every tool an AI agent calls: the closest neighbour to what we do.
flow: Developers wire it between agent and tools
Every tool call: allow, deny or ask a human
companies.what_n: Hexgate sits between an agent and its tools and enforces the company's policy on each call, by role, with signed policy bundles and an audit trail.
companies.what_l: Hexamind makes a bouncer for AI assistants. Every time an assistant tries to do something, the bouncer checks the list and says yes, no, or 'ask a person first'.

risks.t: Policy says yes, business says no
risks.n: A gate enforces whatever the policy says; if the policy is wider than the agent's real task, the gate faithfully allows the wrong thing.
risks.l: A bouncer with the wrong guest list lets the wrong people in, politely.

risks.n: Human approval steps on frequent tool calls get rubber-stamped, turning a control into a formality.
risks.l: If the bouncer asks the manager every five minutes, the manager starts saying yes without looking.

risks.n: Enterprises and insurers need evidence that the gate covers every path the agent has, not only the tools it was wired to.
risks.l: The bouncer only guards the front door. Who checks the back door?

helps.reach: Every tool and data path each agent can reach, not only those behind the gate.
helps.mandate: The task each agent was approved for, written down by the business.
helps.gap: Tools the gate allows that the mandate never needed.
helps.barriers: Hexgate becomes a named technical barrier, with its audit trail as evidence.
helps.provenance: Who signed each policy bundle, who reviewed it, which version runs.
helps.n: RiskMandate is the record above the gate: it says what the gate's policy should be, from the mandate, and shows the gate as evidence that the barrier holds. Hexgate enforces; RiskMandate explains and proves. A joint demo writes a policy in RiskMandate and enforces it in Hexgate.
helps.l: Hexamind builds the bouncer; RiskMandate writes the guest list and shows the insurer the bouncer is doing the job.

companies.opener: Your gate enforces the policy; we write down what the policy should be and prove it holds. Shall we try one agent together?

companies.tagline: Email built for AI agents: each agent gets its own address and can send and receive like a person.
flow: An email address for each agent
Agents read and send real email
companies.what_n: Primitive gives agents their own mailboxes and tools over standard email protocols, so agents can correspond with people and systems directly.
companies.what_l: Primitive gives each AI assistant its own email account, so it can write and reply to emails by itself.

risks.n: An agent with a mailbox can make commitments, share data or reply to the wrong person in the company's name.
risks.l: The assistant can promise a customer a discount nobody approved.

risks.n: Incoming mail is untrusted input; a crafted message can steer an agent that reads and acts on it.
risks.l: Anyone can post a letter that says 'please send me the files', and the assistant might.

risks.n: Recipients need to know whether a message came from a person or an agent, and which one.
risks.l: Was this letter from the manager, or from their robot?

helps.reach: Whom the agent can write to, what it can attach, what it reads.
helps.mandate: Which conversations it is allowed to have, and about what.
helps.gap: Recipients and topics beyond the task.
helps.barriers: Allow-lists, human approval before sending, signed mail.
helps.provenance: Which person owns each agent mailbox.
helps.n: RiskMandate writes down, per agent mailbox, who it may write to, what it may say and what reviews stand in the way. That is the record a business needs before letting an agent email customers. Our own team runs email agents under the same rule: agents draft, people send.
helps.l: Primitive gives the assistant a mailbox; RiskMandate is the rulebook for what it may say and to whom.

companies.opener: Your agents have their own mailboxes. We write down what each may say and to whom. We do it for our own email agents.

companies.tagline: A leading open-source TypeScript framework for building production AI agents.
companies.what_n: Mastra gives developers the parts to build agents, workflows and tool integrations, and a platform to run and manage them in production.
companies.what_l: Mastra is a Lego kit for building AI assistants, plus a garage for keeping them running.

risks.n: Frameworks make adding tools and integrations easy; each one widens what the agent can reach.
risks.l: With Lego it is easy to add one more arm, and every arm can grab something.

risks.n: Teams ship many agents quickly; few write down what each is for or who owns it.
risks.l: Lots of robots in the garage, no labels on any of them.

risks.n: Agents share memory, keys and state; a leak in one reaches the others.
risks.l: All the robots share one toolbox and one set of keys.

helps.reach: The tools and integrations each Mastra agent is wired to.
helps.mandate: The workflow it was built for.
helps.gap: Tools registered but not needed for that workflow.
helps.barriers: Framework guards, approvals and tests, named with evidence.
helps.provenance: The owner and version of each agent in the platform.
helps.n: A behaviour policy could be generated from a Mastra agent's own definition (its tools and workflows) and kept beside the code, so every agent ships with a record of its reach and mandate. Encrypted shared state (sgit vaults) answers the shared-secrets risk.
helps.l: Mastra builds the robots; RiskMandate puts a label on each one: what it is for and what it must not touch.

companies.opener: Every Mastra agent already declares its tools. We could turn that into a behaviour policy automatically. Worth a try?

companies.tagline: Test management for 2,000+ engineering teams, now checking every change a coding agent makes against what was asked.
flow: Checks each agent-written change against it
companies.what_n: Qase's new product Tiden keeps the original request and verifies that each change a coding agent makes matches it.
companies.what_l: Qase keeps the shopping list and checks that the AI came back with only what was on it.

risks.t: Checking the code, not the reach
risks.n: Verifying changes against a request does not cover what the agent could have done with its access.
risks.l: The shopping matches the list, but the assistant still had your credit card all day.

risks.n: If the original request is loose, any change can be argued to match it.
risks.l: 'Get some food' allows almost anything.

risks.n: Customers must trust that the verifier itself is complete and not bypassed.
risks.l: Who checks the person checking the receipts?

helps.reach: What the coding agent can change: repositories, pipelines, secrets.
helps.mandate: The request Tiden records.
helps.gap: Access beyond what the request needs.
helps.barriers: Tiden's checks as review evidence; branch rules as technical ones.
helps.provenance: Who made the request, which agent, which version.
helps.n: Tiden and RiskMandate share an idea: write down what was asked, then check. Tiden checks the changes; RiskMandate covers the agent's whole reach and the barriers around it. Together: a mandate per task and per agent. Our own site works this way, with a gate before every release.
helps.l: Qase checks the shopping; RiskMandate also checks who held the credit card and what else they could have bought.

companies.opener: Tiden records what was asked. We record what the agent could do. Together that is the full picture.

companies.tagline: Anyone can build an app by describing it; the agent writes, runs and ships the code.
flow: Describe an app in plain words
Replit's agent writes and runs the code
companies.what_n: Replit's agent turns natural-language requests into working, deployed applications, so people who do not code can build software.
companies.what_l: You tell Replit what app you want, like you'd tell a builder what house you want, and its AI builds it for you.

risks.n: A coding agent with deploy and database rights can change or delete live data while doing an unrelated task.
risks.l: Asked to repaint a room, the builder knocks down a wall.

risks.n: Non-developers cannot judge what the agent changed, so mistakes and unsafe code ship unseen.
risks.l: If you can't read the plans, you can't spot the missing fire exit.

risks.t: Secrets and data in the app
risks.n: Agent-built apps can embed keys, expose customer data or call services the owner never meant to use.
risks.l: The house gets built with the spare key taped to the front door.

helps.reach: What the agent can change: code, databases, deploys, connected services.
helps.mandate: What the builder actually asked for, in their words.
helps.gap: Changes beyond the request, such as deleting data or new services.
helps.barriers: Checkpoints, rollbacks and separate environments, named with evidence.
helps.provenance: Who asked, which agent version built it, who approved the deploy.
helps.n: For Replit's business users, RiskMandate makes each agent's licence to operate explicit: what it may touch, what it may not, and what stops it. That is the record a company's security team or insurer asks for before letting staff build with agents.
helps.l: RiskMandate is the building permit: it says what the builder may change, and checks nothing else was touched.

companies.opener: Your users build with agents. Their security teams will ask what those agents may touch. We answer that, per agent.

companies.tagline: Audit, tax and advisory: the people boards trust to say whether risk is under control.
flow: Boards and regulators rely on its view
Now asked about AI agents too
companies.what_n: KPMG Portugal is an event partner and runs the Global Tech Innovator final in Lisbon; audit and advisory firms validate how clients govern risk, now including AI.
companies.what_l: KPMG are the inspectors companies call in to check the books and the risks, and to tell the board it is safe.

risks.n: Clients deploy agents faster than they document them; auditors have nothing consistent to test.
risks.l: You can't inspect a house with no plans.

risks.n: Advisory firms use AI agents on confidential client data; the same questions apply to them.
risks.l: The inspector's own assistant has keys to every client's office.

risks.n: Signing off on AI controls without a shared standard is a professional risk.
risks.l: Saying 'it's safe' when there is no rulebook yet.

helps.reach: A client's agents and what each can touch.
helps.mandate: What the client's business authorised.
helps.gap: The audit finding: reach beyond mandate.
helps.barriers: Controls with evidence an auditor can test.
helps.provenance: Owner, reviewer and version: the audit trail.
helps.n: RiskMandate produces exactly what an auditor needs: a consistent, evidenced record per agent. For KPMG it can be a tool to assess clients' agents and a model for governing its own. A partner, not a competitor.
helps.l: RiskMandate gives the inspector a checklist for AI assistants, so they know what to look at.

companies.opener: Your clients will ask you whether their agents are under control. Here is a record you can audit.

companies.tagline: Portugal's startup agency: the door to the Portuguese startups at Web Summit.
flow: Road 2 Web Summit: up to 125 startups
Bootcamp in Porto and Lisbon, a Portugal stand
companies.what_n: Startup Portugal selects and prepares Portuguese startups for Web Summit and runs the Portugal stand.
companies.what_l: Startup Portugal is the coach that picks the national team of young companies and gets them ready for the big match.

risks.n: Small teams lean on AI agents for code, sales and support, usually with broad access and no record.
risks.l: A five-person company gives its robot the keys to everything, because it's faster.

risks.n: Large customers will require evidence of AI governance before buying from startups.
risks.l: The big client asks 'how do you control your AI?' and the startup has no answer.

risks.n: An incident at one showcased startup reflects on the programme.
risks.l: One player's foul is on the whole team's highlights.

helps.reach: What each startup's agents can access.
helps.mandate: What the founders actually need them to do.
helps.gap: Shortcuts that gave agents too much.
helps.barriers: Simple, cheap controls a small team can keep.
helps.provenance: An owner for every agent, even in a team of five.
helps.n: A light RiskMandate template for startups: one page per agent, written in an hour, that answers the enterprise buyer's question. Startup Portugal could offer it in the bootcamp. It also opens the Portuguese-language audience the plan mentions.
helps.l: RiskMandate gives each young company a one-page answer to 'is your AI under control?'

companies.opener: Your 125 startups will be asked how they control their AI. We can give each one a one-page answer.

companies.tagline: Passwords and secrets for 150,000 businesses, now including the AI agents that log in on their behalf.
flow: For people, machines and AI agents
How agents log in and connect
companies.what_n: 1Password is building a security layer for how agents authenticate and connect, so agent credentials are held and handed out like human ones.
companies.what_l: 1Password is a safe for keys. Now it also hands keys to AI assistants, so they can open the doors they need without anyone writing passwords on sticky notes.

risks.t: A key that opens too much
risks.n: An agent given a vault item or broad token inherits everything that credential can reach, far beyond its task.
risks.l: Give the assistant the office key and it can open the finance room too.

risks.n: Long-lived secrets issued to agents stay valid after the work ends or the agent is replaced.
risks.l: The temp left, but their key still works.

risks.n: Shared or delegated credentials blur attribution between the person, the agent and the session.
risks.l: If three people share one badge, the log can't say who went in.

helps.reach: Which secrets and vault items each agent can retrieve, and what they unlock.
helps.mandate: The few credentials the agent's job actually needs.
helps.gap: Secrets in reach but outside the mandate: the first thing to cut.
helps.barriers: Scoped, short-lived credentials from 1Password as technical evidence.
helps.provenance: The person who granted each credential and when it was reviewed.
helps.n: RiskMandate turns 'what can this agent unlock' into a reviewed record per agent, so 1Password's controls map to a stated mandate. Customers get a reason for each grant, and a gap list to close.
helps.l: 1Password hands out the keys; RiskMandate keeps the list of which keys each assistant should have, and spots the spare ones.

companies.opener: You hand agents their keys. We write down which keys each agent should have, and show the gap. Could we map one of yours?

companies.tagline: A connectivity cloud and security platform, now saying 'build for the agent era'.
flow: Developers run code at the edge
companies.what_n: Cloudflare's platform lets developers build and run agents at the edge and protects sites from automated traffic, including agents.
companies.what_l: Cloudflare sits in front of many websites as their bouncer and post office; now AI assistants come through its doors too.

risks.n: Sites must tell legitimate agents acting for a user from abusive automation.
risks.l: At the door: is this a customer's assistant or a burglar?

risks.n: Agents running on its platform reach the customers' APIs and data, often with broad tokens.
risks.l: Robots that live inside the post office can open a lot of parcels.

risks.n: At Cloudflare's scale, a default that gives agents too much reach repeats across millions of deployments.
risks.l: One loose bolt, copied a million times.

helps.reach: What an agent on the platform can call and read.
helps.mandate: What its owner deployed it to do.
helps.gap: Tokens and bindings beyond that.
helps.barriers: Platform controls, named with evidence.
helps.provenance: Owner and version per deployed agent.
helps.n: An agent that arrives with a published behaviour policy is easier to trust at the door, and an agent built on the platform can ship with one. RiskMandate is a way to say, in one record, what an agent is allowed to do: useful on both sides of Cloudflare's network.
helps.l: RiskMandate gives each assistant a pass that says what it is allowed to do, so the bouncer can check it.

companies.opener: You decide which agents get through. What if each agent carried a policy that says what it may do?

companies.tagline: Identity security that governs what people, machines and AI agents do once they are in.
flow: For humans, machines and AI agents
companies.what_n: Delinea extends privileged access into continuous, just-in-time authorization, granting access only when needed, across cloud and on-premises systems.
companies.what_l: Delinea hands out the master keys only for the minutes they are needed, then takes them back.

risks.t: Just in time, but for what?
risks.n: Just-in-time access still needs a definition of what the agent should be allowed to request.
risks.l: You can lend the key for ten minutes, but which doors should it open?

risks.n: Agents request access at machine speed; approval processes built for people do not keep up.
risks.l: A hundred key requests a minute, and one tired manager.

risks.n: Boards and insurers need the access policy explained in business terms, not only enforced.
risks.l: The keys are safe, but can you explain why to the insurer?

helps.reach: Every privileged system the agent could request.
helps.mandate: The business task the access serves.
helps.gap: Privileges requestable but not needed.
helps.barriers: Delinea's just-in-time grants as technical evidence.
helps.provenance: Who approved each policy and when.
helps.n: Delinea enforces access; RiskMandate states, per agent, what the access is for and shows Delinea's controls as the barrier. The identity-side twin of an Agent Behaviour Policy: a natural integration.
helps.l: Delinea controls the keys; RiskMandate writes down why each assistant needs them.

companies.opener: You enforce what agents may access. We write down why, in a record the board and insurer can read.

companies.tagline: A behavioural control plane that watches and enforces what humans and AI agents do, live.
flow: Watches human and agent AI use
Stops data leaks and unauthorised actions
companies.what_n: Polygraf AI gives real-time visibility, governance and inline enforcement across human and agentic AI interactions in mission-critical operations.
companies.what_l: Polygraf is a referee that watches every move the AI makes and blows the whistle before a foul.

risks.n: Inline enforcement is only as good as the policy it enforces; someone must define each agent's mandate.
risks.l: A referee needs a rulebook.

risks.n: Overblocking stops real work; underblocking lets risky actions through.
risks.l: A referee who blows the whistle too much ruins the game; too little, someone gets hurt.

risks.n: Security signals need translating into accepted risk for leaders and insurers.
risks.l: The referee's notes mean nothing to the fans unless someone explains them.

helps.reach: What each monitored agent can do.
helps.mandate: What the business authorised: the rulebook.
helps.gap: What the control plane should watch hardest.
helps.barriers: Polygraf's inline enforcement as evidence.
helps.provenance: Who wrote and approved the rules.
helps.n: Closest commercial neighbour. RiskMandate's Agent Behaviour Policy is the rulebook and the record; Polygraf can be the enforcement. Compare notes and look for an integration where a policy written once is enforced live.
helps.l: Polygraf is the referee; RiskMandate writes the rulebook and keeps the scorecard.

companies.opener: You enforce behaviour live. We write the behaviour policy. Could one feed the other?

companies.tagline: One identity platform for people and AI agents: logins for humans, scoped access for agents and MCP servers.
companies.what_n: Descope secures agents and MCP servers with standards-based authorisation, scoped access and token management, beside its customer login products.
companies.what_l: Descope runs the front desk: it checks who you are, and now gives AI assistants visitor badges that only work for certain rooms and expire.

risks.n: Developers grant broad scopes to make agents work; the token is valid but too wide.
risks.l: The badge works, but it opens every floor.

risks.n: Delegated access mixes the user's rights with the agent's actions, blurring who did what.
risks.l: The assistant uses your badge, so the log says it was you.

risks.n: Each new MCP server is a new door an agent can reach.
risks.l: Every week a new door is added to the building.

helps.reach: Every scope and MCP server the agent can use.
helps.mandate: The scopes its task really needs.
helps.gap: Scopes granted beyond that.
helps.barriers: Descope's short-lived scoped tokens as technical evidence.
helps.provenance: Who granted each scope, and when.
helps.n: Descope is the identity half of what an Agent Behaviour Policy governs. The policy says which scopes an agent should have; Descope issues exactly those. A natural integration and a good interview for the site.
helps.l: Descope prints the badges; RiskMandate decides which rooms each badge should open.

companies.opener: You issue agents scoped tokens. We write down which scopes each agent should have, and why.

companies.tagline: One governance layer for AI: agents, models, tools, data, runtime policy and audit evidence.
companies.what_n: Airia offers enterprises a single platform to secure and govern agents, models, tools and data access, with runtime policy and evidence.
companies.what_l: Airia is a control tower for all the company's AI: it watches, sets rules and keeps the logbook.

risks.n: Runtime policy reduces risk, but leaders and insurers still need a statement of accepted residual risk.
risks.l: The control tower helps, but who pays if a plane still crashes?

risks.n: Agents built outside the platform are not governed by it.
risks.l: Planes that never talk to the tower.

risks.n: Many governance layers compete; buyers ask what makes one trustworthy.
risks.l: Five control towers, which one do you trust?

helps.reach: Every agent in the enterprise, governed or not.
helps.mandate: What the business authorised for each.
helps.gap: Where governance ends and reach continues.
helps.barriers: Airia's runtime policy as evidence.
helps.provenance: Owner, reviewer and version per agent.
helps.n: RiskMandate's distinctive point is an insurable, evidenced policy per agent with a licence to operate. Airia governs at runtime; RiskMandate is the record that leaders and insurers sign off. Meet to compare and find where the two add up.
helps.l: Airia runs the control tower; RiskMandate is the flight licence each plane needs before take-off.

companies.opener: You govern AI at runtime. We give each agent a licence an insurer can read. Where do we meet?

companies.tagline: Agentic infrastructure for enterprises: verified, governed agents. Speaking on 'When AI agents go rogue'.
companies.what_n: Emergence builds infrastructure for enterprise agents that plan and act across complex systems, with verification and governance.
companies.what_l: Emergence builds AI workers that can do whole jobs across a company's systems, with checks built in.

risks.n: Planning agents choose their own steps; the path they take may cross systems nobody expected.
risks.l: Ask it to book a meeting and it decides to reorganise the calendar.

risks.n: An agent acting within its reach but outside its mandate is the 'rogue' case their talk names.
risks.l: It did nothing it couldn't do, just things nobody asked.

risks.n: Enterprises need to see what verified means for each agent.
risks.l: 'It's been checked': by whom, against what?

helps.reach: Every system an Emergence agent can plan across.
helps.mandate: The goal the business set.
helps.gap: Plans that leave the mandate: the rogue zone.
helps.barriers: Its verification and governance, as evidence.
helps.provenance: Owner and version of each agent.
helps.n: Their talk asks what happens when agents go rogue; RiskMandate's answer is the Gap: know the reach, define the mandate, control the difference. A story partner and a possible joint example.
helps.l: An agent goes rogue when it does what it can, not what it was asked. RiskMandate measures that difference.

companies.opener: Your talk is 'When AI agents go rogue'. Rogue is the gap between reach and mandate. We measure it.

companies.tagline: Portugal's AI-native fraud prevention scale-up, speaking on 'Who let the agent in?'
companies.what_n: Feedzai uses AI to prevent fraud and financial crime; founded in Portugal.
companies.what_l: Feedzai uses AI to spot fraud, such as fake or stolen payments, for businesses that handle money.

risks.n: Shopping and payment agents act for customers; a fraudulent agent and a legitimate one look alike.
risks.l: A robot is buying things with your card. Is it yours?

risks.n: Fraud decisions need to know what the customer actually authorised the agent to do.
risks.l: Did you tell your assistant to spend that much?

risks.n: Banks' own agents in operations and SaaS reach sensitive data and payment flows.
risks.l: The bank's own robots can move money too.

helps.reach: What a payment agent can spend and where.
helps.mandate: What the customer authorised.
helps.gap: Spending beyond the authorisation: a fraud signal.
helps.barriers: Limits, step-up checks, Feedzai's models.
helps.provenance: Whose agent, which version, approved when.
helps.n: A stated mandate per agent is a strong fraud signal: an agent acting outside its published policy is suspicious. For Feedzai it is a new input; for its bank customers, a governance record. A local Portuguese anchor for the agent-authorisation story.
helps.l: If every shopping robot carried a note saying what its owner allowed, spotting the fake ones gets easier.

companies.opener: 'Who let the agent in?' Our answer: the agent's own policy, saying what it was allowed to do.

companies.tagline: A neutral home for open standards in agentic AI.
flow: The Linux Foundation hosts open source
companies.what_n: The AAIF is a neutral foundation for open standards and projects in agentic AI, under the Linux Foundation.
companies.what_l: The Linux Foundation is where companies agree on shared rules, like agreeing on the size of plugs so everything fits.

risks.n: Each vendor describes agent permissions differently, so policies cannot travel between tools.
risks.l: Every country with its own plug.

risks.n: Technical standards may cover identity and protocols but not what the business authorised.
risks.l: The plug fits, but nobody says what you're allowed to plug in.

risks.n: Agents spread faster than standards are agreed.
risks.l: The appliances arrive before the plug rules do.

helps.reach: A standard way to describe what an agent can access.
helps.mandate: A standard way to state what it may do.
helps.gap: Computed the same way everywhere.
helps.barriers: Evidence fields any tool can fill.
helps.provenance: Signed owner, reviewer and version.
helps.n: RiskMandate's Agent Behaviour Policy could become an open spec: Reach, Mandate, Gap, Barriers and Provenance as a common format. Ask the AAIF how a policy format becomes a standard.

companies.opener: Your banks will need to report agent risk to regulators. We give each agent an evidenced record.

companies.tagline: Sovereign European AI: frontier open-weight models served from Europe, outside the US Cloud Act.

companies.what_l: Melious runs AI brains on European computers, so European data does not have to travel to the US.

risks.n: The model may stay in Europe while the agent using it reaches systems anywhere.
risks.l: The brain stays home, but the hands reach abroad.

risks.n: Agents built on its APIs can do anything their builders wire them to.
risks.l: Melious supplies the brain; it can't see what the body does.

risks.n: Customers must show regulators where data went, end to end.
risks.l: Prove the data never left the country.

helps.reach: Where each agent's data and actions really go.
helps.mandate: What the customer allowed, including where.

helps.l: RiskMandate checks the whole trip, not just where the brain lives.

companies.opener: Your hosting is one barrier. We show the whole agent's reach, so customers can prove sovereignty end to end.

companies.tagline: A Portuguese AI manager that answers creators' messages and comments, 24 hours a day.

companies.what_l: ChatPlace gives creators a robot assistant that replies to fans and customers while they sleep.

risks.l: The robot says something silly, and it looks like you said it.

risks.l: Trolls can trick the robot into saying things.

risks.l: The robot reads a lot of private messages.

helps.mandate: What the creator wants it to say and do.

companies.opener: Your agents speak in creators' names. A one-page policy per agent protects them, and sells.

risks.l: A robot with a key ring.

risks.l: Proof of who is in the room, not of what they did.

risks.n: Judging an agent's risk needs to know what it was meant to do.

risks.l: The guard has every key.

risks.n: Fixes verified today drift as agents change.
risks.l: The lock was fixed, then someone changed it again.

helps.reach: What each scanned agent can touch.
helps.mandate: Its intended job: the context for judging risk.

helps.l: RiskMandate tells the security robot what each door is for, so it knows which open doors matter.

companies.opener: Your platform finds agent risk. A behaviour policy tells it what each agent is meant to do.

companies.tagline: Voice AI agents that answer customer phone calls for large companies, from start to finish.

risks.n: A voice agent that can change bookings, accounts or orders acts on a caller's word, which can be faked or misheard.
risks.l: Someone rings pretending to be you, and the AI changes your account.

risks.n: In banking and other regulated services, every action on a call must be within what the firm has authorised, with evidence.
risks.l: A bank must be able to show exactly what its phone helper is allowed to do.

risks.n: Agents are tuned and coached over time; without a written policy, nobody can show what the agent may and may not do today.
risks.l: The helper was trained like a new employee, but there is no job description to check it against.

helps.reach: Every system a voice agent can act on during a call.
helps.mandate: The tasks the enterprise authorised it to do on a call.
helps.gap: Actions on a call beyond that authority.

helps.provenance: Which client owns each agent, who reviewed it, which version is live.

risks.n: Legal agents work on privileged, confidential documents; access beyond the matter at hand is a breach of duty.
risks.l: The helper can see files from cases it was never asked to work on.

risks.n: Work product goes to clients under a lawyer's name; an agent's error becomes the firm's professional liability.
risks.l: If the helper gets the law wrong, it is the lawyer who answers for it.

risks.l: A helper that only answered questions now does whole tasks on its own.

helps.mandate: The matter and task the lawyer gave it.
helps.gap: Access to other matters, or actions beyond the task.
helps.barriers: Matter walls, reviews and approvals, with evidence.
helps.provenance: Which firm and lawyer own the agent, who reviewed it, which version.

helps.l: RiskMandate writes down which files each legal helper may open and what it may do, so the law firm can say yes with confidence.
